title: The Psychology of Data Visualization
text:
Themes
If a picture’s worth a thousand words (Wikipedia contributors, 2024), what exactly does it say? This course will focus on the psychology of data visualization—how to read, critique, and generate meaningful figures that inform but don’t mislead. We’ll take inspiration from recognized classic figures and unpack what makes them exemplary. We’ll critique figures that deliberately or inadvertently mislead or confuse. We’ll learn what 150 years of vision science, the foundation of experimental psychology, has to say about data visualization. And we’ll learn how to build our own reproducible figures using Python, R, and JavaScript. No prior programming experience is required.

title: Capturing images
text: This short tutorial shows how to capture images in web pages and how to make screenshots on Mac OS and Windows OS.

title: Capturing images
text:
Capturing images in web pages
Most browsers support “right-clicking”, clicking on the right button of a multibutton mouse (or the equivalent motion on a trackpad) when you hover over an image.
Using Chrome on Mac OS for example, I visited the Penn State homepage at https://www.psu.edu. In mousing over a photo, I right clicked and had the following panel appear:






Figure 1: Image from psu.edu in Chrome using MacOS



Note that there are several options. I find that these are the most useful:

“Open Image in New Tab”. I often do this to make sure that the web page link (URL) actually contains the image I want it to. Then I switch to that tab for further steps.
“Save Image As…”. This is useful if you want to download a local copy.
“Copy Image Address”. Use this for capturing URLs of images, but not the images themselves.

Here is an illustration of the same process on Windows 11:






Figure 2: Image from psu.edu on Chrome using Windows 11



Not that the pop-up has similar options.






WarningWord to the wise



Some websites do not support this feature. That’s why I prefer to use “open image in new tab” to see if I’m actually capturing what I want to capture. As a back-up, you can usually resort to your computer’s built-in screen capture tool that we’ll describe next.

title: Capturing images
text:
Capturing images on your screen
When the image you want is not a static image, you may need to use your computer’s screen capture tool.
From the same Penn State home page, I try right-clicking on the top “hero” animation. This is the result.






Figure 3: Results of right-clicking on psu.edu ‘hero’ image/animation.



Notice that the pop-up window does not have the same menu items as it did for a static image. Of course, this is an animation, and so it’s not that surprising that things would differ. Let’s say I want to capture a static image from this animation.

Press the screen capture keystroke combination for your computer. On Mac OS, you have two choices, command+shift+3 (pressed simultaneously) immediately takes a screenshot of your entire window.







Figure 4: Capturing entire screen on Mac OS using command+shift+3.



Note that to capture a specific segment of a video, you have to wait until that image appears and press these keys quickly.

As an alternative on Mac OS, you can use command+shift+4. Then, you click and drag your mouse to indicate the region of the screen you want to capture. When the image appears in the animation, just release the mouse button and that image will be captured.







Figure 5: Capturing a segment of the screen on Mac OS using command+shift+4.









NoteUnder construction



Instructions about how to do this on Windows are a work-in-progress.

title: Captions and figure numbers
text:
Figure captions
There are several ways to add captions to your Quarto figures depending on how the figures are generated.

R code chunk
If you create a figure using an R code chunk, you can add a caption by using the fig-caption argument in the code chunk options. See Figure 1.



```{r}
#| label: fig-my-plot
#| fig-cap: "This is my plot. I hope that you like it."

x_random <- rnorm(n = 100)
random_df <- data.frame(x = x_random)

random_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Random Data") + 
  theme_minimal()
```


Figure 1: This code shows how to add parameters to an R code chunk. The parameters are preceded by #|. The parameter values are specified as key-value pairs. The key is the label before the colon :, and the value is what follows the colon We need to label figures using #| label: fig-<name>, where the figure name is specified as fig-<name>; here it is my-plot. This makes sure that your Quarto document assigns a unique name to your figure. We also need a #| fig-cap: parameter (cap is short for caption) to add a caption.



The figure rendered by Figure 1 is as follows:


Code
x_random <- rnorm(n = 100)
random_df <- data.frame(x = x_random)

random_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Random Data") + 
  theme_minimal()


`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.








Figure 2: This is my plot. I hope that you like it.











NoteTitles can coexist with captions.



We can make figures with titles using labs(title = "Histogram of Random Data") or the ggtitle() function. The same figure can have a caption added using fig-cap: "This is a caption" in the chunk options.




Images
If you include an image from the internet or a local file, it’s easy to add a caption.
The syntax for adding an image is ![Caption goes  here](url_or_path_to_file_goes_here).
So the following:
![Nittany Lion Shrine from brand.psu.edu.](https://brand.psu.edu/images/backgrounds/warneke-shrine_v1_1.jpg)
yields



Nittany Lion Shrine from brand.psu.edu.








ImportantWhere did the figure number go?



Notice that the above image does not have a figure number, unlike the previous ones. What gives?
The answer is that we need to give the figure its own unique #fig-<name> identifer.


To give an included or embedded image a sequential figure number, we need to add something to the Quarto code that embeds the image. You might have to scroll horizontally to see all of the code.
![Nittany Lion Shrine from brand.psu.edu.](https://brand.psu.edu/images/backgrounds/warneke-shrine_v1_1.jpg){#fig-lion-shrine}
Now that our embedded figure has its own #fig-name, Quarto gives it a sequential figure number. See Figure 3) below.






Figure 3: Nittany Lion Shrine from brand.psu.edu.





Videos, code chunks, etc.
You can turn many bits of Quarto code into figures using a special syntax that wraps the code in pairs of triple colons ::: as shown in Figure 4.



::: {#fig-video}

Then you might add some text explaining what the first plot is about. For example, you could describe the data being visualized and the purpose of the plot.
Here, we’re going to use the diamonds dataset the is built in to ggplot2.
Create an R chunk as follows:

```{r}
  aes(x = price) +
  geom_histogram()
```


Figure 6: Simple ggplot2 syntax to plot a histogram of the price variable in the diamonds dataset.









WarningSyntax slip-ups



90+% of frustrations with computers are because we don’t tell them exactly what they need to know.
A code chunk in Quarto starts with triple backticks and ends with triple backticks.
The {r} tells Quarto that the code chunk is written in R.
Quarto understands other programming languages, so this is important.


Save and render your Quarto document.

The resulting web page should look something like this:






Figure 8: Quarto document rendered after Figure 01 code is executed.




Unpacking ggplot syntax
To make a figure, we need a dataset formatted as a data frame. The diamonds dataset is already in the right format.
In our plotting code illustrated in Figure 6, we call the ggplot() function and specify the dataset to plot using the data=diamonds parameter2.
Next, we ‘add’ a layer to our figure using the + command. That layer contains the ‘aesthetics’ or mapping between our dataset and some feature of the figure (e.g., x position, y position, fill color, etc.) We specify these mappings using the aes() command. For this specific figure, we’re mapping x position on the figure to the price variable in the dataset.
Finally, our figure needs a ‘geom’, a geometric object or format for the figure. We have a single variable (price), and we want to plot a histogram of it, so we add (+) use the geom_histogram().

`binwidth` and `bins`








Figure 15: Output from the code in Figure 14.





That also looks good. Notice that the data are plotted in terms of the order of the color variable, not the category of the variable with the largest number of cases (G). The plot of cut naturally sorted in the same order as the underlying order of cut.
How would we reorder the plot from highest to lowest?
There are several ways to do this. We’re going to use a scheme that will be useful to you in the future.
First, we need to install two new packages. Switch to your R console to do this.



install.packages(c("dplyr", "forcats"))


Figure 16: Code to install the dplyr and forcats packages.



Then, in your Quarto document, add a line to the code chunk in your Setup section so that it looks like the following:



## Setup

Load required packages into the workspace.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)
```


Figure 17: Quarto (and R) code to put at the top of your document so that these libraries are available for later chunks.



With those preliminaries finished, we can now use these libraries to sort the diamonds color data for our summary figure.
Here is the code to add to your Quarto document.



```{r}
diamonds |>
  mutate(color_ct = fct_infreq(color)) |>
                                        
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = color_ct) +
  geom_histogram(stat = "count")

```


Figure 18: Code to render a sorted histogram/barplot of the color variable.



Let’s unpack what’s happening here. First, we give ggplot2 input using a new command, the pipe (|>). Think of the pipe as passing data to the next step. Next, the mutate() function creates a new variable called color_ct, short for color count. The value of color_ct comes from fct_infreq(color), a function in the forcats package. This package has all kinds of useful tools for manipulating factors, both ordered and unordered discrete variable. Learn more about it here. The mutate() command creates a new variable called color_ct using fct_infreq(color) and adds it to the dataset. We then pipe/pass this augmented dataset to ggplot, and the rest should be familiar to you already.

1diamonds |>
2  mutate(color_ct = fct_infreq(color)) |>
  
  ggplot() +
3  aes(x = color_ct) +
  geom_histogram(stat = "count")


1

Pipe/send the diamonds dataset using the pipe |> command.

2

Use mutate() from dplyr and fct_infreq() from forcats to create a new variable called color_ct.

3

Use the new color_ct variable to make the histogram.










Figure 19: Output from the code in Figure 18.











ImportantSorting in a different direction



Read the documentation for the fct_infreq() to see if you can figure out how to print the bars from low to high.
Hint: It involves the use of another forcats function called fct_rev().


If our category labels are more than single letters, it can be easier to rotate the figure. Here’s an easy way to do that.

diamonds |>                               
  mutate(color_ct = fct_infreq(color)) |> 
  
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = color_ct) +                     
  geom_histogram(stat = "count") +
1  coord_flip()


1

“Flip” the coordinates so that the bars are horizontal.










Figure 20: Output from the code in Figure 18.





Let’s put the highest count on top.



```{r}
diamonds |>                               
  mutate(color_ct = fct_rev(fct_infreq(color))) |>
  
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = color_ct) +                     
  geom_histogram(stat = "count") +
  coord_flip()                    
```


Figure 21: Code to flip the coordinates of our histogram.



The following shows what this should look like.

diamonds |>                               
1  mutate(color_ct = fct_rev(fct_infreq(color))) |>
  
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = color_ct) +                     
  geom_histogram(stat = "count") +
  coord_flip()                    


1

Reverse the sort order using fct_rev().










Figure 22: Output from the code in Figure 21.











ImportantWork iteratively



Making figures with code forces us to work one step at a time. That’s a good discipline, but can frustrate people who like to move quickly.
My recommendations are to create the most basic figure for your purpose, then add features (sorting, flipping coordinates, adding color, etc.) one by one. In fact, if you create separate figures for each new addition, then you can always go back to where you started.

text:
Nominal data
Let’s focus on nominal or categorical data, specifically the favorite colors of some imaginary set of people.


Code
# Make an array of color names
colors <- c("red", "orange", "yellow", "green", "cyan", "blue", "violet", "white", "black", "gray")


There are n=10 colors in this set.






NoteYour turn



Why are these data nominal or nominally scaled? Or rather, why aren’t they ordinal, interval, or ratio?



Generating
For demonstration purposes, we want to take some number of random samples of these colors. Let’s pick n=200 and sample with replacement (replace=TRUE in the code below), meaning that we could have any number of colors in our sample of 200 imaginary people.


Code
# Use `sample()` to pick a random sample of these *with* replacement so that 
# the numbers/color differ.

our_color_sample

Summarizing
What can we say to summarize categorical data?
We can report the number of total responses.


Code
length(our_color_sample)


[1] 200


We can report the number of unique categories.


Code
length(unique(our_color_sample))


[1] 10


We can report the number of responses per category.


Code
colors_df <- data.frame(favorite_color = our_color_sample)

xtabs(formula = ~favorite_color, data = colors_df)


favorite_color

Visualizing
Single nominal variables don’t offer us many options for visualization. A bar plot showing the number of observations in each category seems to be it.


Code
colors_df |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count")








Figure 1: A black and white barplot of the random favorite color data





We can also add colors to the bars.


Code
colors_df |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color, fill = favorite_color) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_discrete_manual(aesthetics = c("color", "fill"),
                        values = sort(colors))








Figure 2: A colorful barplot of the random favorite color data





We can think of this as mapping the name of the color category in our data to the way that category is represented in our figure.






flowchart LR
  A[Value of `favorite_color` in dataset] --> B(Actual color of bar in the figure.)




Figure 3





We can flip the axis just for fun. Which is more readable?

Horizontal barplot


Code
colors_df |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color, fill = favorite_color) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip()








Figure 4: A colorful horizontal barplot of the random favorite color data







Bar/column with textures
Sometimes we don’t want to use color to distinguish nominal categories.


Code
colors_df |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color, fill = favorite_color) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = after_stat(count))) +
  scale_fill_pattern() + # from package 'fillpattern' 
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 5: A barplot of the random favorite color data using textures





Or, we want to use some different textures and have control over them.


Code
colors_xtab <- data.frame(table(colors_df))
names(colors_xtab) <- c("favorite_color", "count")

colors_xtab |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color, y = count) +
  # From package 'ggpattern'
  # See https://r-graph-gallery.com/368-black-and-white-barchart.html
  geom_col_pattern(
    aes(
      pattern = favorite_color,
      pattern_angle = favorite_color,
      pattern_spacing = favorite_color
    ),
    fill = 'white',
    color = 'black',
    pattern_density = 0.5,
    pattern_fill = 'black',
    pattern_color = 'darkgrey'
  )








Figure 6: A barplot of the random favorite color data using textures







Ordered
It can be useful to sort the counts of nominal variables to faciliate comparisons among categories.


Code
colors_df |>
  count(favorite_color) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  mutate(favorite_color = factor(favorite_color, levels = favorite_color)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = n), stat = "identity")








Figure 7: A horizontal barplot of the random favorite color data, sorted











Important



First, we use the count() function to count the number of responses for each favorite color. The counts per color category are in a new variable called n.
Next, we sort the data table by the n column, using the arrange(desc(n)) commmand. This says we are ordering the data in descending order of the counts.
Then, we use the mutate() function to change the favorite_color variable in the dataset to an arranged/sorted one based on counts.


Let’s order the other ones while we’re at it.


Code
colors_df |>
  count(favorite_color) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  mutate(favorite_color = factor(favorite_color, levels = favorite_color)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color, y = n, fill = favorite_color) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_pattern() + # from package 'fillpattern'
  theme(legend.position = "none") 








Figure 8: A barplot of the random favorite color data using textures







Code
colors_df |>
  count(favorite_color) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  mutate(favorite_color = factor(favorite_color, levels = favorite_color)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color, y = n) +
  # From package 'ggpattern'
  # See https://r-graph-gallery.com/368-black-and-white-barchart.html
  geom_col_pattern(
    aes(
      pattern = favorite_color,
      pattern_angle = favorite_color,
      pattern_spacing = favorite_color
    ),
    fill = 'white',
    color = 'black',
    pattern_density = 0.5,
    pattern_fill = 'black',
    pattern_color = 'darkgrey'
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 9: A barplot of the random favorite color data using textures







Lollipop chart
The lollipop chart uses less ink, so the ink/data ratio (Tufte, 2001) is higher than with barplots.


Code
colors_df |>
  count(favorite_color) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  mutate(favorite_color = factor(favorite_color, levels = favorite_color)) |>
  ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(
    x = favorite_color,
    y = n,
    color = favorite_color,
    fill = favorite_color
  )) +
  geom_segment(aes(
    x = favorite_color,
    xend = favorite_color,
    y = 0,
    yend = n,
    color = favorite_color
  )) +
  scale_color_identity() +
  scale_fill_identity()








Figure 10: A lollipop plot of the random favorite color data







Stacked barplot
We can also stack them.


Code
colors_df |>
  count(favorite_color) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = "", y = n, fill = favorite_color) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  xlab("")








Figure 11: A stacked barplot of the random favorite color data





This makes more sense with another nominal variable in the mix.
Let’s add a ‘school’ variable.


Code
school <- sample(c("psu", "osu", "mich", "usc"), size=200, replace=TRUE)
colors_school_df <- colors_df
colors_school_df$school <- school


Then create the plot.


Code
colors_school_xtab <- data.frame(table(colors_school_df))
names(colors_school_xtab) <- c("favorite_color", "school", "count")

# colors_school_xtab |>
#   ggplot() +
#   aes(x = school, y=count, fill = favorite_color) +
#   scale_fill_identity() +
#   geom_bar(stat="identity", position="stack")

colors_school_df |> 
  count(school, favorite_color) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  aes(school, n, fill = favorite_color) + 
  scale_fill_identity() + 
  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="stack")








Figure 12: A stacked barplot of the random favorite color data







Stacked barplot alternative


Code
colors_school_xtab |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color, y=count, fill = school) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="stack")








Figure 13: Another stacked barplot of the random favorite color data.







Dodged barplot
Using the ‘dodge’ parameter is another way to show data with two categorical variables.


Code
colors_school_xtab |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = school, y=count, fill = favorite_color) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge")








Figure 14: A horizontal barplot of the random favorite color data







Pie chart


Code
colors_xtab <- data.frame(table(colors_df))
names(colors_xtab) <- c("favorite_color", "count")

colors_xtab |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = count, fill = favorite_color)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  scale_fill_identity()








Figure 15: A piechart of the random favorite color data







Ring chart


Code
# https://r-graph-gallery.com/128-ring-or-donut-plot.html

# Compute percentages
colors_xtab$fraction = colors_xtab$count / sum(colors_xtab$count)

# Compute the cumulative percentages (top of each rectangle)
colors_xtab$ymax = cumsum(colors_xtab$fraction)

# Compute the bottom of each rectangle
colors_xtab$ymin = c(0, head(colors_xtab$ymax, n = -1))

# Make the plot
colors_xtab |>
  ggplot(aes(
    ymax = ymax,
    ymin = ymin,
    xmax = 4,
    xmin = 3,
    fill = favorite_color
  )) +
  geom_rect() +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") + # Try to remove that to understand how the chart is built initially
  xlim(c(2, 4)) + # Try to remove that to see how to make a pie chart
  scale_fill_identity()








Figure 16: A ring/donut chart of the random favorite color data







Mosaic plot


Code
ggplot(data = colors_school_df) +
  geom_mosaic(aes(x = product(favorite_color, school), fill = favorite_color)) +   
  labs(y="Favorite", x="School", title = "Favorite colors by school") +
  scale_fill_identity()








Figure 17: A mosaic chart of the random favorite color by school data

title: Making and visualizing data
text:
Ordinal data
We usually consider colors as nominal or categorical variables. But the physical input to the visual system is continuous.



https://rmit.pressbooks.pub/colourtheory1/part/2-colour-theory-the-visible-spectrum/


The continuous variable that underlies color is wavelength, a property of electromagnetic radiation. The human visual system maps patterns of physical wavelength to the psychological dimension of color.
Curiously, human color perception shows that this psychological mapping wraps in a circular way that physical wavelength does not.



https://pixabay.com/vectors/rainbow-colors-circle-color-spectrum-154569/



Generating
But rather than dive down that particular rat hole now, let’s make some ordinal data from the random color dataset. Imagine that we had n=50 participants and each gave a rating to these colors. The ratings had numbers, with 1 assigned to the participant’s first choice, and 4 assigned to the fourth choice. We won’t keep track of the specific users at this point.


Code
ratings <- c("1st", "2nd", "3rd", "4th")

our_rating_sample <- sample(ratings, size=200, replace=TRUE)
colors_rating_df <- colors_df
colors_rating_df$rating <- our_rating_sample

colors_rating_xtab <- data.frame(table(colors_rating_df))
names(colors_rating_xtab) <- c("favorite_color", "rating", "count")




Visualizing
Many of the same plot types are available for ordinal data.

Bar plot ordinal dodge


Code
colors_rating_xtab |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x=rating, y=count, fill = favorite_color) +
  # aes(x = favorite_color, y = school, fill = favorite_color) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge")








Figure 18: A barplot of the random favorite color data with an ordinal rating







Bar plot ordinal stacked


Code
# colors_rating_xtab |>
#   ggplot() +
#   aes(x=favorite_color, y=count, fill = favorite_color) +
#   scale_fill_identity() +
#   geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge")

colors_rating_xtab |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = rating, y=count, fill = favorite_color) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="stack")








Figure 19: A stacked barplot of the random favorite color data with an ordinal rating







Bar plot ordinal stacked alternative


Code
colors_rating_xtab |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = favorite_color, y=count, fill = rating) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="stack")








Figure 20: Another stacked barplot of the random favorite color data with an ordinal rating

title: Making and visualizing data
text:
Continuous data

Generating
Let’s imagine that we are studying a group of people who vary in age and body temperature.
We’ll assume that they are healthy–fever free.
And we assume that we’re sampling uniformly across children (0-18 years) and adults (18-85).






Important



Kids and adults have different typical body temperatures!
https://www.webmd.com/first-aid/normal-body-temperature




Code
n_kids <- 100
n_adults <- 100
age_days_kids <- runif(n_kids, 0, 18*365)
age_days_adults <- runif(n_adults, 18*365+1, 85*365)

# https://www.webmd.com/first-aid/normal-body-temperature
body_temps_kids <- runif(n_kids, 95.9, 99.5)
body_temps_adults <- runif(n_adults, 97, 99)

age_days <- c(age_days_kids, age_days_adults)
body_temp_F <- c(body_temps_kids, body_temps_adults)

age_temp_df <- data.frame(age_days = age_days, body_temp = body_temp_F)

# Mix them up a bit
age_temp_df <- age_temp_df[sample(nrow(age_temp_df)),]




Visualizing
To visualize continuous data, we have to decide what question(s) we want to answer.

Scatterplot
The simplest visualization of two continuous variables is a scatterplot.


Code
age_temp_df |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = age_days, y = body_temp) +
  geom_point()








Figure 21: A scatterplot of the age and body temperature data.







Histograms


Code
age_temp_df |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = age_days) +
  geom_histogram()


`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.








Figure 22: A histogram of the age data.







Code
age_temp_df |>
  ggplot() +

Order of operations






Note



Installing R and RStudio Desktop is usually straightforward, but glitches arise from time to time. If something’s not working, try to seek help from an expert friend or the internet. If you get frustrated, stop. We’ll spend time in-class helping with troubleshooting.


You must install R first.

Installing R

Visit https://cran.r-project.org







Figure 1: https://lib.stat.cmu.edu/R/CRAN/




Click on the “Download R for…” link appropriate for the operating system of your computer, proably Windows or macOS.


If you have a newer Mac, you want the version “For Apple Silicon”: R-4.6.1-arm64







ImportantConfirm your macOS operating system and hardware



Click on the Apple Menu in the upper left hand corner. Open the “About this Mac” menu item. A window will open.






Figure 2



Note that the operating system and hardware are displayed here. Under Chip, the “Apple M2 Pro” means that my laptop is using Apple Silicon. The macOS value says “Tahoe 26.6.1”. R-4.6.1 works with all macOS > 14 (Sonoma).



If you are on Windows, click on the “install R for the first time” link. Then download R-4.6.1 for Windows.


After you’ve downloaded the installer program. Open it. It is usually found in the default location for file downloads, often in a folder called “Downloads.”
Open the installer program and follow the directions.



Installing RStudio Desktop
Next install RStudio Desktop. Visit https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/#rstudio-ide-oss-downloads.
MacOS users select RStudio-2026.07.1-147.dmg and Windows Users select RStudio-2026.07.1-147.exe.
When the programs download, run the installation programs.

Open RStudio Desktop.

If RStudio Desktop opens successfully, do the computer happy dance.
